I've noticed that Groundhogs like to survey their surroundings from an elevated position, even climbing trees and fence posts to do so at times. But - they can really hug the ground as they make a hasty loping retreat to their den if they feel threatened by a situation.

description:
Weather: 
It was an early spring-like day in Northwestern PA with a high of 67°F and a low of 35°F. The winds were around 10-14 mph. It was partly cloudy throughout the day until the clouds became overcast.

I believe it is the marmots monax based off the research done at the University of Wisconsin Stevens Point: vertebrate collection. There was a moment where I thought it was an Eastern Cottontail (sylvilagus floridanus) due to the similar skull structure.

The skull measurements are:
- 3.25” long
- 2” wide
- Top teeth: .5” 
(This is based off what skull parts are shown)

I think the Groundhog enjoyed his simple life by the agricultural water flow down by the road. It was a beautiful area where he got to wake up and eat all the fresh vegetation given. His home was about 8 inches wide, but wide enough for it to not be safe.
The day came where he could have been attacked by his predator the Red-Tailed Hawk (buteo jamaicensis) or the Bald Eagle (haliaeetus leucocephalus) or even a Red Fox (vulpes vulpes) who have been known to the area. But who knows what actually happened to him or was it really a him? All I can say is that some college kid found him for a species account.

description:
This was a fun find at a MWTP gathering at Mississippi Gateway Regional Park.

Looking at the track by the ruler:
-The overall track is fan-shaped: a wide arc at the toes, narrowing to a rounded heel. 
-Track measurements: Length 2 3/4”, Width 2”
-This track shows five bulbous toe pads with sharp nails, arranged in 1-3-1 toe pattern. This is classic squirrel hind track morphology, though it's beyond the maximum length of 2 1/2” inches recorded for gray squirrel hinds.
-Metatarsal pads are fainter than the toe divots, but are present in an arc from under toe 1 (furthest from scale) through toe 4. The outer edge of the foot registers from toe 5 down into the tarsal pad (heel), which registers as a deep divot, just before the edge of the mud.

Looking to the left:
-There are three parallel claw marks in the edge of the mud. These appear to be toes 2-4 of the left hind foot. Toes 1 and 5 are also visible in the muddy waters.

Looking above the left hind track:
-There’s a magnificent double-circle imprint, with four clear claw imprints above it. Classic squirrel front track morphology shows four toes with claws, a trapezoidal metacarpal (palm) pad, and large paired heel pads behind the palm — and this substrate only took clear imprints of the four nails and large, paired heel pads.

Morphology and size point to our largest squirrel in this region: Marmota monax. 

This particular park appears to be a good place to find woodchuck tracks now, as we found recently used burrows downslope and additional sets of prints around the muddy, disturbed areas of this park.

California Ground Squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi) The "squirrel's upper parts are mottled, with the fur containing a mixture of gray, light brown and dusky hairs. The shoulders, neck and sides are a lighter gray. The fur around the eyes is whitish. The underside is lighter, buff or grayish yellow. Head and body are about 30 cm (12 in) long and the tail an additional 15 centimetres (5.9 in). They can weigh from 280 to 738 g (9.9 to 26.0 oz). The tail is relatively bushy for a ground squirrel, and at a quick glance, the squirrel might be mistaken for a fox squirrel.
As is typical for ground squirrels, California ground squirrels live in burrows, which they excavate themselves. Some burrows are occupied communally, but each squirrel has its own entrance. Although they readily become tame in areas used by humans, and quickly learn to take food left or offered by picnickers, they spend most of their time within 25 m (80 ft) of their burrows, and rarely go further than 50 m (160 ft) from it.
In the colder parts of their range, California ground squirrels hibernate for several months, but in areas where winters have no snow, most squirrels are active year-round."

description:
A last-minute trip to the NJ pine barrens from Philadelphia. Cami, Hirdi and Mika wanted to do a few museums in Philly so I ran off to do some iNatting. I checked the internet for good natural areas near Philly and realized the pine barrens were within 30 miles. I went with a trail I found online (Mullica River Trail (yellow blaze), accessible from the parking area next to the Ranger Station at Atsion (marked as Atsion Office on Google Maps). It was described as having typical pine barrens habitat and was a lot of fun to explore. I was blitzing from around 11AM-5PM and then on the way back got stuck in the worst traffic jam I have ever been in while crossing the Benjamin Franklin Bridge. They closed it down due to police activity and it ended up taking me an extra hour and a half to reroute to the Whitman bridge.

description:
California ground squirrel is digging a burrow under the coyote brush shrub nearby.

California Ground Squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi) The "squirrel's upper parts are mottled, with the fur containing a mixture of gray, light brown and dusky hairs. The shoulders, neck and sides are a lighter gray. The fur around the eyes is whitish. The underside is lighter, buff or grayish yellow. Head and body are about 30 cm (12 in) long and the tail an additional 15 centimetres (5.9 in). They can weigh from 280 to 738 g (9.9 to 26.0 oz). The tail is relatively bushy for a ground squirrel, and at a quick glance, the squirrel might be mistaken for a fox squirrel.
As is typical for ground squirrels, California ground squirrels live in burrows, which they excavate themselves. Some burrows are occupied communally, but each squirrel has its own entrance. Although they readily become tame in areas used by humans, and quickly learn to take food left or offered by picnickers, they spend most of their time within 25 m (80 ft) of their burrows, and rarely go further than 50 m (160 ft) from it.
In the colder parts of their range, California ground squirrels hibernate for several months, but in areas where winters have no snow, most squirrels are active year-round."
